Introduction to zisar

Source: vignettes/zisar.Rmd
zisar.Rmd

Spatial count data often have more zeros than a count distribution allows, more variance than the mean, and dependence between neighbouring units: the number of solar panels installed in a neighbourhood, of emergency visits from a municipality, of firms of a sector in a district. The ZISAR model handles the three at once, and zisar estimates it by maximum likelihood.

library(zisar)

The model

For nn spatial units linked by a weights matrix WW (row-standardised, with zero diagonal), the log-mean of the counts follows a simultaneous autoregressive (SAR) process with unit-level random effects,

η=ρWη+Xβ+u,u∼N(0,σ2I),soη=(I−ρW)−1(Xβ+u). \eta = \rho W \eta + X\beta + u, \qquad u \sim N(0, \sigma^2 I), \qquad\text{so}\qquad \eta = (I - \rho W)^{-1}(X\beta + u).

Each count is a structural zero with probability πi\pi_i, and otherwise negative binomial with mean μi=exp⁡(ηi)\mu_i = \exp(\eta_i) and shape κ\kappa:

yi∼πi1{yi=0}+(1−πi)NB(μi,κ),logit(πi)=zi′γ. y_i \sim \pi_i \, 1\{y_i = 0\} + (1 - \pi_i)\,\mathrm{NB}(\mu_i, \kappa), \qquad \mathrm{logit}(\pi_i) = z_i'\gamma.

A zero can come from either part of the mixture. A structural zero comes from a unit that is out of the process altogether, with probability πi\pi_i; a sampling zero from a unit in the process whose negative binomial count happens to be zero. Only the second kind carries information on ηi\eta_i, and the model tells them apart through the covariates ziz_i and through the intensity of the neighbours.

The spatial multiplier (I−ρW)−1(I - \rho W)^{-1} carries a change in the predictor of one unit to all the others: the effect decays with the number of steps in WW, at a rate set by ρ\rho. With ρ=0.2\rho = 0.2 it stays within the first ring of neighbours; with ρ=0.8\rho = 0.8 it covers the whole lattice.

The multiplier acts on the latent predictor, not on the observed counts, so the model has no endogenous regressor and is estimated by maximum likelihood. Overdispersion has three sources: the negative binomial shape κ\kappa, the structural zeros πi\pi_i and the random effects σ\sigma. The latent field is integrated out with the Laplace approximation in TMB.

This is the restricted model: the structural zeros depend on covariates only. The general model adds a spatial field to the inflation predictor, for zeros that cluster in space; see below.

Fitting a model

rzisar() simulates data on a regular lattice with queen contiguity. Here 400 units, a spatial parameter of 0.5, two covariates in the count process and one in the zero-inflation process:

set.seed(2026)
sim <- rzisar(20, beta = c(0.5, 0.6, -0.4), rho = 0.5, gamma = c(-1, 0.9),
              kappa = 2, sigma = 0.4)
head(sim$data)
#>   y       x1      x2      z1
#> 1 1  0.52059  1.3369 -1.6053
#> 2 2 -1.07969  0.5527 -0.5025
#> 3 2  0.13924 -1.0565 -1.1959
#> 4 0 -0.08475 -0.1902 -1.0711
#> 5 6 -0.66664 -0.9092  0.7462
#> 6 0 -2.51609 -2.0009 -0.4369
mean(sim$data$y == 0)
#> [1] 0.465

zisar() takes a two-part formula: the terms before | enter the count process, those after it the zero-inflation process. W can be a base matrix, a sparse Matrix, or an spdep listw object, with rows in the order of the data.

fit <- zisar(y ~ x1 + x2 | z1, data = sim$data, W = sim$W)
summary(fit)
#> 
#> Call:
#> zisar(formula = y ~ x1 + x2 | z1, data = sim$data, W = sim$W)
#> 
#> 400 spatial units, 46.5% zeros
#> 
#> Count model coefficients (SAR negative binomial, log link):
#>             Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
#> (Intercept)   0.3558     0.0905    3.93  8.5e-05 ***
#> x1            0.5918     0.0736    8.04  9.2e-16 ***
#> x2           -0.5495     0.0746   -7.37  1.7e-13 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> Zero-inflation model coefficients (binomial, logit link):
#>             Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
#> (Intercept)   -1.179      0.282   -4.18  2.9e-05 ***
#> z1             0.995      0.229    4.35  1.4e-05 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> Spatial and dispersion parameters:
#>       Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
#> rho     0.6060     0.0972    6.24  4.5e-10 ***
#> kappa   2.0203     0.7320                     
#> sigma   0.3486     0.1223                     
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> Log-likelihood (Laplace): -736.74 on 8 Df
#> AIC: 1489.5   BIC: 1521.4
#> Log-determinant: eigen.  Optimiser: converged after 30 iterations.

The estimates are close to the values used in the simulation (β=(0.5,0.6,−0.4)\beta = (0.5, 0.6, -0.4), γ=(−1,0.9)\gamma = (-1, 0.9), ρ=0.5\rho = 0.5, κ=2\kappa = 2, σ=0.4\sigma = 0.4). The usual accessors work:

coef(fit)
#> count_(Intercept)          count_x1          count_x2  zero_(Intercept) 
#>            0.3558            0.5918           -0.5495           -1.1794 
#>           zero_z1               rho 
#>            0.9947            0.6060
sqrt(diag(vcov(fit)))
#> count_(Intercept)          count_x1          count_x2  zero_(Intercept) 
#>           0.09055           0.07363           0.07458           0.28232 
#>           zero_z1               rho 
#>           0.22871           0.09717
logLik(fit)
#> 'log Lik.' -736.7 (df=8)
AIC(fit)
#> [1] 1489

A formula without | uses the same terms in both processes, y ~ x | 1 gives a constant inflation probability, and an offset() term in the count part enters the log-mean with coefficient one, for exposures: y ~ x1 + offset(log(households)) | z1.

Spatial weights from real geography

With polygons, spdep builds the weights; pass the listw object (or the matrix) to zisar(). Every unit must have a row in the data: units cannot be dropped, because they all enter the spatial multiplier.

library(sf)
library(spdep)
areas <- st_read("areas.gpkg")
nb <- poly2nb(areas, queen = TRUE)
lw <- nb2listw(nb, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)
fit <- zisar(y ~ x1 + x2 | z1, data = areas, W = lw)

Direct, indirect and total effects

In a spatial model a coefficient is not the effect of its covariate: a change in one unit moves the expected count there (direct effect) and, through the spatial multiplier, in the other units (indirect effect, or spillover). zisar_effects() averages them over units, with simulation standard errors:

zisar_effects(fit, B = 100)
#> ZISAR average effects on E[y] (simulation SEs, B = 100)
#> 
#>              Direct         Indirect            Total
#> x1  1.6312 (0.2927)  2.2126 (0.9602)  3.8438 (1.1102)
#> x2 -1.5147 (0.2520) -2.0545 (0.7905) -3.5692 (0.8750)
#> z1 -0.5911 (0.1170)  0.0000 (0.0000) -0.5911 (0.1170)

z1 acts only through the probability of a structural zero, which concerns the unit itself: its indirect effect is zero. A covariate entering both processes (the same name in both parts of the formula) combines the two channels.

Counterfactual scenarios

predict() gives the fitted means (type = "response"), the means of the count component ("count"), the inflation probabilities ("zero") or the latent field ("eta"). With newdata for the same units it computes a scenario: here x1 rises by one in a single unit, and the expected counts of its neighbours rise as well.

nd <- sim$data
nd$x1[190] <- nd$x1[190] + 1
change <- predict(fit, newdata = nd) - predict(fit)
round(change[c(190, which(sim$W[190, ] > 0))], 3)
#> [1] 1.615 0.064 0.083 0.016 0.193 0.211 0.256 0.264 0.054
sum(change)
#> [1] 3.594

Comparing models

fixed holds parameters at given values. With ρ=0\rho = 0 and σ\sigma close to zero the model reduces to the aspatial zero-inflated negative binomial, the same model as pscl::zeroinfl(dist = "negbin"):

fit_zinb <- zisar(y ~ x1 + x2 | z1, data = sim$data, W = sim$W,
                  fixed = list(rho = 0, sigma = 0.001))
AIC(fit_zinb, fit)
#>          df  AIC
#> fit_zinb  6 1507
#> fit       8 1489

The test of ρ=0\rho = 0 is in the summary (Wald). The aspatial model with random effects (fixed = list(rho = 0)) is nested in ZISAR, but on spatially dependent data it is often not estimable: the random effects have to absorb the spatial structure, σ\sigma grows, and the Laplace approximation breaks down (see below).

Clustered structural zeros

In the restricted model, structural zeros depend on ziz_i only. When whole areas are out of the market (a planning restriction, no supplier nearby), the zeros cluster beyond what the covariates explain, and the inflation predictor needs a spatial structure of its own. zero_spatial selects it.

The natural choice is a SAR field with one value per unit, logit(πi)=zi′γ+gi\mathrm{logit}(\pi_i) = z_i'\gamma + g_i with g=(I−ρ0W)−1e0g = (I - \rho_0 W)^{-1} e_0, e0∼N(0,σ02I)e_0 \sim N(0, \sigma_0^2 I), independent of uu (zero_spatial = "field"). Its Laplace approximation fails: each gig_i is informed by a single outcome that is zero or not, the error of the approximation accumulates over the nn values of the field, and on data without any field the likelihood-ratio statistic against the restricted model can reach the thousands. The package fits it, but does not recommend it.

The reduced-rank field (zero_spatial = "reduced") puts the SAR field on the KK knots of a lattice instead, g=Bαg = B\alpha with α=(I−ρ0WK)−1e0\alpha = (I - \rho_0 W_K)^{-1} e_0, and spreads each knot value over the units nearby through the basis BB. Each knot value is informed by many units, and the approximation holds. zisar_basis() builds the knots and the basis from the coordinates of the units and a knot spacing, which sets the resolution of the field. Here the data come from a unit-level field, and the reduced-rank field on knots four cells apart recovers it:

set.seed(3)
sim0 <- rzisar(20, beta = c(1, 0.5), rho = 0.4, gamma = c(-0.5, 0.8),
               zero_spatial = "field", rho0 = 0.9, sigma0 = 0.6)
b <- zisar_basis(sim0$coords, h = 4)
b
#> Reduced-rank basis: 36 knots, spacing 4, radius 6, 400 units (6.2 knots per unit)
fit_r <- zisar(y ~ x1 | z1, data = sim0$data, W = sim0$W)
fit_g <- zisar(y ~ x1 | z1, data = sim0$data, W = sim0$W,
               zero_spatial = "reduced", basis = b)
#> Warning: The optimum has a large gradient (69100). It may be a spurious optimum
#> of the Laplace approximation, or a genuine one with structural zeros among
#> units of high intensity. Refit to data simulated from this fit to tell them
#> apart, and use a parametric bootstrap for standard errors; see ?zisar.
#> Warning: The Hessian is not positive definite: standard errors are not
#> available. The model may be over-parameterised, or the optimum on a boundary.
summary(fit_g)$spatial
#>                    Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)
#> rho                0.126781         NA      NA       NA
#> kappa             53.584810         NA      NA       NA
#> sigma              0.982232         NA      NA       NA
#> rho0.rho0_raw      0.000606         NA      NA       NA
#> sigma0.log_sigma0  1.114305         NA      NA       NA
cor(fit_g$g, sim0$g)
#> [1] 0.5161

The fit starts from the restricted model: the likelihood of the general model is evaluated on a grid of (ρ0,σ0)(\rho_0, \sigma_0) with the other parameters at the restricted estimates, and the optimiser starts from the best point. The grid is kept in fit_g$field_profile; a gain that never rises above zero means the data hold no field.

The restricted model is the general one with σ0=0\sigma_0 = 0, on the boundary of the parameter space, so the likelihood-ratio statistic has a mixture distribution and the χ22\chi^2_2 p-value is conservative:

lr <- 2 * (logLik(fit_g) - logLik(fit_r))
pchisq(as.numeric(lr), df = 2, lower.tail = FALSE)
#> [1] 8.41e-05

zero_spatial = "sar" is a different mechanism, without random effects: a SAR filter on the predictor, logit(π)=(I−ρ0W)−1Zγ\mathrm{logit}(\pi) = (I - \rho_0 W)^{-1} Z\gamma, so that the inflation covariates of a unit’s neighbours shift its probability of a structural zero, and zisar_effects() reports spillovers for them too.

When the Laplace approximation breaks down

For a zero count, the conditional distribution of ηi\eta_i can be bimodal: the zero is either structural (and μi\mu_i can be large) or negative binomial (and μi\mu_i is small). This produces spurious optima, with a huge gradient and sometimes a positive log-likelihood, mostly in small samples, with misspecified models (an omitted covariate) and with the unit-level inflation field. zisar() checks every fit, restarts from other values when a check fails, and warns if no clean optimum is found; fit$laplace_ok records the outcome and summary() reports it.

fit$laplace_ok
#> [1] TRUE
fit$max_grad
#> [1] 0.000214

A large gradient is not always spurious. When structural zeros occur among units of high intensity, the bimodality is part of the model and the genuine optimum has a large gradient too. A positive log-likelihood is always spurious; a large gradient is told apart by refitting the model to data simulated from the fit, which share the gradient if it is genuine. Standard errors then come from a parametric bootstrap, with each refit started from the estimates:

st <- list(beta = coef(fit, "count"), gamma = coef(fit, "zero"),
           rho = fit$rho, kappa = fit$kappa, sigma = fit$sigma)
ys <- simulate(fit, nsim = 100, seed = 1)
boot <- sapply(ys, function(y) {
  d <- sim$data
  d$y <- y
  coef(suppressWarnings(zisar(y ~ x1 + x2 | z1, data = d, W = sim$W,
                              start = st, restarts = FALSE)))
})
apply(boot, 1, sd)

Large data sets

The log-determinant log⁡|I−ρW|\log|I - \rho W| is computed from the eigenvalues of WW for up to 5000 units, and from a sparse Cholesky factorisation beyond (logdet = "sparse"), which keeps memory and time manageable for tens of thousands of units. zisar_effects() never forms the dense n×nn \times n multiplier either.

fit <- zisar(y ~ x1 + x2 | z1, data = big, W = W_big, logdet = "sparse")

Reference

Salvini, N., Arbia, G. and Nardelli, V. (2026). ZISAR: A zero-inflated spatial autoregressive model for count data with random effects. Working paper, Università Cattolica del Sacro Cuore.
